## What you will learn

- Compute a covariance matrix from data and read variances, standard deviations and correlations out of it.
- Draw (and interpret) the 95% uncertainty ellipse of a 2D position estimate from its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
- Propagate uncertainty through a linear or linearized function with $\Sigma' = J\,\Sigma\,J^\top$ and check it with Monte Carlo.
- Sample correlated noise with a Cholesky factor and test measurements with the Mahalanobis distance.
- Fill and read the 6×6 covariance array in ROS 2 pose and odometry messages.

## Why it matters

After karmel drives 1 m forward, where is it? Not "at (1, 0)" but "near (1, 0), with about ±1 cm uncertainty along the direction of travel and ±3.5 cm sideways". The sideways uncertainty is bigger because a 2° heading error swings the endpoint left or right. Describing that needs more than one σ per axis: it needs to know how the x and y errors *move together*. That is covariance.

Covariance is the language of state estimation. The IMU message carries covariance matrices ([07.06](../../07-sensors/07.06-imu-in-ros2.md)), odometry uncertainty grows as a covariance ([09.06](../../09-odometry/09.06-accumulated-error.md)), localization draws covariance ellipses ([10.02](../../10-localization/10.02-uncertainty-gaussians.md)), and the multivariate and extended Kalman filters ([10.05](../../10-localization/10.05-kalman-filter-multivariate.md), [10.06](../../10-localization/10.06-extended-kalman-filter.md)) are, mechanically, a sequence of $J\Sigma J^\top$ and matrix inversions. Particle filters ([10.08](../../10-localization/10.08-particle-filter-mcl.md)) sample from these Gaussians, and pose-graph SLAM ([11.05](../../11-slam/11.05-pose-graphs-loop-closure.md)) weighs every constraint by an inverse covariance. PCA in the ML track ([FML.11](../machine-learning/FML.11-unsupervised-learning.md)) is the eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix. You need [FM.14](FM.14-distributions-gaussians-noise.md) (σ, variance, Gaussian) and [FM.07](FM.07-matrices.md) (matrix multiplication, transpose, inverse).

## Concept

Drive karmel 1 m forward 1,000 times and mark where it stops. The marks form a cloud. Measured along the direction of travel, the cloud is narrow: wheel encoders measure distance well. Measured sideways, it is wide: a small heading error at the start becomes a big sideways error at the end. The cloud is an **ellipse**, long across the path, short along it.

Now drive diagonally (45°). The same ellipse is rotated. If you only record "σ of x" and "σ of y" you get about 26 mm for both, which makes the cloud look like a circle — you have thrown away the shape. What you lost is the fact that when x is too big, y tends to be too small: the errors are **correlated**. Covariance is the number that records this "moving together".

**Covariance** between two quantities is positive when they tend to be above their means at the same time, negative when one is above while the other is below, and zero when there is no linear relationship. Dividing it by both standard deviations gives the **correlation coefficient** ρ, between −1 and +1, which is easier to read: ρ = −0.85 means "strongly opposite", independent of units.

A **covariance matrix** collects all of these for a state vector. For a 2D position it is 2×2: variances on the diagonal, covariance off the diagonal (twice, because covariance is symmetric). For a pose $(x, y, \theta)$ it is 3×3; ROS uses 6×6 for $(x, y, z, \text{roll}, \text{pitch}, \text{yaw})$.

A **multivariate Gaussian** is the bell curve in several dimensions, fully described by a mean vector and a covariance matrix. Its contours of equal probability are ellipses (ellipsoids in 3D). The ellipse's axes point along the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and their lengths are proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues. That is how every "uncertainty ellipse" in RViz is drawn.

The most useful operation: when you push a Gaussian through a (linearized) function, the new covariance is $J\Sigma J^\top$, where $J$ is the matrix of derivatives. This is how the Kalman filter predicts that uncertainty grows as the robot moves. If this is the part that feels like magic, ask:

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "Walk me through $\Sigma' = J\Sigma J^\top$ for a robot driving 1 m with 2° heading noise, with numbers, and show me why the sideways uncertainty is $d\cdot\sigma_\theta$."

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — Covariance and correlation

For two random variables:

$$\operatorname{cov}(X, Y) = E[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)], \qquad \rho_{XY} = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y} \in [-1, 1]$$

From $N$ samples: $\operatorname{cov} \approx \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$. Note $\operatorname{cov}(X, X) = \sigma_X^2$.

**Numerical example.** Five position errors in mm: (2, 1), (−1, −2), (0, 1), (3, 4), (−4, −4). Means are both 0. Then $\sigma_x^2 = (4+1+0+9+16)/4 = 7.5$, $\sigma_y^2 = (1+4+1+16+16)/4 = 9.5$, $\operatorname{cov} = (2+2+0+12+16)/4 = 8.0$, and $\rho = 8.0/\sqrt{7.5 \cdot 9.5} = 0.948$: when x is off, y is off in the same direction.

Independence implies zero covariance. The converse is false in general ($Y = X^2$ with symmetric $X$ has zero covariance but is totally dependent), but **for jointly Gaussian variables zero covariance does mean independence**.

### Level 2 — The covariance matrix and the multivariate Gaussian

For a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with mean $\boldsymbol\mu$:

$$\Sigma = E[(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top], \qquad \Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{cov}(x_i, x_j)$$

Properties you can check on any matrix someone hands you:
- **Symmetric**: $\Sigma = \Sigma^\top$.
- **Positive semi-definite** (PSD): all eigenvalues ≥ 0, equivalently $\mathbf{v}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{v} \geq 0$ for every $\mathbf{v}$ (a variance can't be negative in any direction). Implies $|\Sigma_{ij}| \leq \sqrt{\Sigma_{ii}\Sigma_{jj}}$, i.e. $|\rho| \leq 1$.

The multivariate Gaussian density:

$$p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^n \det\Sigma}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)\right)$$

The quadratic form in the exponent is the squared **Mahalanobis distance** $d_M^2$: distance measured in "σ units along each direction of the ellipse". Contours of constant $d_M$ are ellipses.

**Marginals are free.** The distribution of a subset of variables is Gaussian with the corresponding sub-block of μ and Σ. The x–y uncertainty of a 3D pose $(x, y, \theta)$ is just the top-left 2×2 block.

**Numerical example — reading a matrix.** $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 0.04 & 0.03 \\ 0.03 & 0.09 \end{bmatrix}$ m². Then $\sigma_x = 0.2$ m, $\sigma_y = 0.3$ m, $\rho = 0.03/(0.2 \cdot 0.3) = 0.5$.

### Level 3 — Ellipses, rotation and propagation

**Uncertainty ellipse.** Eigen-decompose $\Sigma = V\Lambda V^\top$. The ellipse $d_M^2 = k$ has semi-axes $\sqrt{k\lambda_i}$ along eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_i$. In 2D, $d_M^2$ follows a chi-squared distribution with 2 degrees of freedom, so $k = 5.991$ gives the ellipse containing 95% of samples ($k = 1$ contains only 39%, a common surprise).

**Numerical example.** $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \times 10^{-4}$ m² has eigenvalues $8\times10^{-4}$ (eigenvector along 45°) and $2\times10^{-4}$ (along 135°). σ along the axes: 28.3 mm and 14.1 mm. 95% semi-axes: $\sqrt{5.991}\cdot 28.3 = 69.2$ mm and 34.6 mm.

**Linear transformation.** If $\mathbf{y} = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ then

$$\boldsymbol\mu_y = A\boldsymbol\mu_x + \mathbf{b}, \qquad \Sigma_y = A\,\Sigma_x A^\top$$

This is the 1D rule $\sigma_Y = |a|\sigma_X$ grown up. Rotating a covariance from the robot frame to the world frame uses the rotation matrix $R$: $\Sigma_\text{world} = R\,\Sigma_\text{robot} R^\top$.

**Nonlinear functions: linearize.** If $\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x})$ and the uncertainty is small, use the Jacobian $J = \partial f/\partial\mathbf{x}$ (matrix of partial derivatives, see [FM.17](FM.17-derivatives.md)) evaluated at the mean:

$$\Sigma_y \approx J\,\Sigma_x J^\top$$

This is exactly the covariance prediction of the Extended Kalman Filter ([10.06](../../10-localization/10.06-extended-kalman-filter.md)).

**Numerical example — the robot drives 1 m.** Input: distance $d = 1.0$ m with $\sigma_d = 10$ mm, heading $\theta$ with $\sigma_\theta = 2° = 0.0349$ rad. End position: $x = d\cos\theta$, $y = d\sin\theta$. Jacobian with respect to $(d, \theta)$:

$$J = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -d\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & d\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

At $\theta = 0$: $J = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & d \end{bmatrix}$, so $\Sigma_{xy} = \operatorname{diag}(0.010^2,\ (1.0 \cdot 0.0349)^2) = \operatorname{diag}(1.00\times10^{-4},\ 1.2185\times10^{-3})$ m². σ_x = 10.0 mm, σ_y = **34.9 mm**. Sideways error = distance × heading error.

At $\theta = 45°$ the same ellipse rotated: $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 6.592 & -5.592 \\ -5.592 & 6.592 \end{bmatrix}\times10^{-4}$ m², σ_x = σ_y = 25.7 mm, ρ = −0.848, major axis at 135° (perpendicular to travel). A Monte Carlo run of 100,000 simulated drives in the code below gives the same numbers to three digits, and 95.0% of the samples land inside the 95% ellipse.

### Level 4 — Sampling, gating and ROS messages

**Sampling a correlated Gaussian.** Factor $\Sigma = LL^\top$ (Cholesky, $L$ lower-triangular). If $\mathbf{z}$ is a vector of independent standard normals, then $\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol\mu + L\mathbf{z}$ has covariance $L\,I\,L^\top = \Sigma$ (the linear rule again). Cholesky fails when Σ is not positive definite, which makes it a free validity check. This is how a particle filter spreads particles and how a simulator injects correlated noise.

**Gating with the Mahalanobis distance.** Is an observation consistent with the estimate? Compare $d_M^2$ with the chi-squared threshold (5.991 for 95% in 2D). With the heading-0 estimate above, an observation 50 mm *sideways* at (1.00, 0.05) has $d_M = 50/34.9 = 1.43$ → accept. An observation 50 mm *ahead* at (1.05, 0.00) has $d_M = 50/10 = 5.0$ → reject. Same Euclidean distance, opposite decisions, because the estimate is confident along x. Kalman filters and SLAM front-ends use this test to reject wrong data associations.

**ROS 2 covariance arrays.** `geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovariance` stores a 6×6 matrix as `float64[36]`, row-major, in the order $(x, y, z, \text{rot}_X, \text{rot}_Y, \text{rot}_Z)$. Index = `6*row + col`: var x is `[0]`, cov(x, y) is `[1]` and `[6]`, var y is `[7]`, var yaw is `[35]`. `sensor_msgs/msg/Imu` uses 3×3 arrays (index `3*row + col`). An all-zero covariance usually means "unknown", not "perfect" — [07.06](../../07-sensors/07.06-imu-in-ros2.md) covers the conventions.

## Diagram

```text
 Robot drives 1 m along x (heading 0°)           Same drive at heading 45° (world frame)

   y ▲                                            y ▲         major axis at 135°
     │            ╭─╮  ← 95% ellipse                │       ╲   (perpendicular to travel)
     │            │ │    semi-axes:                 │    ╭───╲──╮
     │            │ │    85.4 mm (sideways, y)      │     ╲  •  ╲   σx = σy = 25.7 mm
 ────┼────────────┼•┼──────► x                      │      ╰──╲──╯   ρ = −0.85
     │ start      │ │    24.5 mm (along x)          │   ↗ direction of travel
     │ (0,0)      │ │                               │ ↗
     │            ╰─╯                               •────────────────────► x
     │          (1.0, 0)                          start

 Σ = [ 1.00e-4     0     ]  m²                   Σ = R Σ_robot Rᵀ = [  6.59e-4  −5.59e-4 ]  m²
     [   0     1.2185e-3 ]                                           [ −5.59e-4   6.59e-4 ]

 Propagation pipeline (the EKF prediction in miniature):

 (d, θ) ~ N( [1.0, 0], diag(0.010², 0.0349²) ) ──► f(d,θ) = (d cosθ, d sinθ) ──► Σ_xy ≈ J Σ Jᵀ
                                                     │
                                                     └─ J = ∂f/∂(d,θ) evaluated at the mean
```

## Code

Save as `fm15_covariance.py` and run `python fm15_covariance.py` (numpy + matplotlib). It compares Monte Carlo against the linearized $J\Sigma J^\top$, draws 95% ellipses into `fm15_ellipses.png`, samples with Cholesky, gates with Mahalanobis distance, and fills a ROS-style covariance array.

```python
"""fm15_covariance.py — covariance of a 2D robot position after driving 1 m.

Run:  python fm15_covariance.py      (writes fm15_ellipses.png)
Needs: numpy, matplotlib
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CHI2_2DOF_95 = 5.991  # 95% of a 2D Gaussian lies inside Mahalanobis distance^2 < 5.991


def drive_straight_mc(d: float, sigma_d: float, sigma_theta: float, heading: float,
                      n: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """Monte Carlo: end positions (n x 2) after driving distance d with noisy length and heading."""
    dist = d + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_d, n)
    theta = heading + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_theta, n)
    return np.column_stack((dist * np.cos(theta), dist * np.sin(theta)))


def drive_straight_linearized(d: float, sigma_d: float, sigma_theta: float, heading: float
                              ) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """First-order propagation: Sigma_xy = J Sigma_in J^T, J = d(x,y)/d(dist,theta)."""
    mean = np.array([d * math.cos(heading), d * math.sin(heading)])
    J = np.array([[math.cos(heading), -d * math.sin(heading)],
                  [math.sin(heading),  d * math.cos(heading)]])
    sigma_in = np.diag([sigma_d**2, sigma_theta**2])
    return mean, J @ sigma_in @ J.T


def ellipse_points(mean: np.ndarray, cov: np.ndarray, chi2: float = CHI2_2DOF_95, n: int = 200) -> np.ndarray:
    eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)                # cov = V diag(lambda) V^T
    t = np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, n)
    circle = np.vstack((np.cos(t), np.sin(t)))            # unit circle, 2 x n
    return (mean[:, None] + eigvecs @ (np.sqrt(chi2 * eigvals)[:, None] * circle)).T


def describe(name: str, cov: np.ndarray) -> None:
    sx, sy = math.sqrt(cov[0, 0]), math.sqrt(cov[1, 1])
    rho = cov[0, 1] / (sx * sy)
    eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    major = eigvecs[:, 1]
    angle = math.degrees(math.atan2(major[1], major[0])) % 180
    semi = np.sqrt(CHI2_2DOF_95 * eigvals) * 1000
    print(f"   {name}: sigma_x={sx * 1000:.1f} mm  sigma_y={sy * 1000:.1f} mm  rho={rho:+.3f}  "
          f"95% ellipse semi-axes={semi[1]:.1f} x {semi[0]:.1f} mm, major axis at {angle:.1f} deg")


def main() -> None:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=15)
    d, sigma_d, sigma_theta = 1.0, 0.010, math.radians(2.0)

    print("1) Covariance by hand vs np.cov on 5 samples (mm)")
    xy = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [-1.0, -2.0], [0.0, 1.0], [3.0, 4.0], [-4.0, -4.0]])
    dev = xy - xy.mean(axis=0)
    by_hand = dev.T @ dev / (len(xy) - 1)
    print("   by hand:", by_hand.round(3).tolist(), "  np.cov:", np.cov(xy, rowvar=False).round(3).tolist())

    print("2) Robot drives 1.0 m, sigma_d=10 mm, sigma_theta=2 deg")
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
    for heading_deg, color in ((0.0, "tab:blue"), (45.0, "tab:orange")):
        h = math.radians(heading_deg)
        pts = drive_straight_mc(d, sigma_d, sigma_theta, h, 100_000, rng)
        mean_lin, cov_lin = drive_straight_linearized(d, sigma_d, sigma_theta, h)
        cov_mc = np.cov(pts, rowvar=False)
        print(f"  heading {heading_deg:.0f} deg")
        print("   Monte Carlo cov [m^2]:", np.array2string(cov_mc, precision=7, suppress_small=True).replace("\n", ""))
        print("   J Sigma J^T cov [m^2]:", np.array2string(cov_lin, precision=7, suppress_small=True).replace("\n", ""))
        describe("Monte Carlo", cov_mc)
        describe("linearized ", cov_lin)
        inside = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", pts - mean_lin, np.linalg.inv(cov_lin), pts - mean_lin) < CHI2_2DOF_95
        print(f"   fraction of samples inside the 95% ellipse: {inside.mean():.3f}")
        ax.scatter(pts[:2000, 0], pts[:2000, 1], s=2, alpha=0.3, color=color)
        e = ellipse_points(mean_lin, cov_lin)
        ax.plot(e[:, 0], e[:, 1], color=color, lw=2, label=f"heading {heading_deg:.0f} deg, 95% ellipse")

    print("3) Rotating a covariance: Sigma_world = R Sigma_robot R^T")
    cov_robot = np.diag([sigma_d**2, (d * sigma_theta) ** 2])
    c, s = math.cos(math.radians(45)), math.sin(math.radians(45))
    R = np.array([[c, -s], [s, c]])
    print("   R Sigma R^T at 45 deg [m^2]:", np.array2string(R @ cov_robot @ R.T, precision=7).replace("\n", ""))

    print("4) Sampling a correlated Gaussian with Cholesky: x = mu + L z")
    mu = np.array([0.707, 0.707])
    cov = R @ cov_robot @ R.T
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(cov)
    samples = mu + rng.standard_normal((200_000, 2)) @ L.T
    print("   sample cov [m^2]:", np.array2string(np.cov(samples, rowvar=False), precision=7).replace("\n", ""))

    print("5) Mahalanobis distance: is a landmark observation consistent with the estimate?")
    mean0, cov0 = drive_straight_linearized(d, sigma_d, sigma_theta, 0.0)
    for obs in (np.array([1.00, 0.05]), np.array([1.05, 0.00])):
        diff = obs - mean0
        m2 = diff @ np.linalg.solve(cov0, diff)
        print(f"   obs {obs.tolist()}: euclidean={np.linalg.norm(diff) * 1000:.0f} mm  "
              f"mahalanobis={math.sqrt(m2):.2f}  {'accept' if m2 < CHI2_2DOF_95 else 'REJECT'} (d^2 < 5.991)")

    print("6) ROS geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovariance: 6x6 row-major, order x y z roll pitch yaw")
    cov6 = np.zeros((6, 6))
    cov6[:2, :2] = cov0
    cov6[5, 5] = sigma_theta**2
    flat = cov6.flatten().tolist()
    print(f"   covariance[0]={flat[0]:.6f} (var x)  [7]={flat[7]:.6f} (var y)  [35]={flat[35]:.6f} (var yaw)")

    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("x [m]")
    ax.set_ylabel("y [m]")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(OUT / "fm15_ellipses.png", dpi=120)
    print("wrote fm15_ellipses.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Output (numpy 2.x, seed 15):

`fm15_ellipses.png` shows two thin clouds of dots: one around (1, 0) stretched vertically, one around (0.71, 0.71) stretched along the 135° diagonal, each hugged by its 95% ellipse. (Var y and var yaw print the same value only because $d = 1$ m: $\sigma_y = d\,\sigma_\theta$.)

## Exercise

All exercises need hardware: **none**.

### Exercise FM.15-E1 — Read a covariance matrix `[numerical]`

Goal: extract σ and ρ without code.
An estimator publishes $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 0.04 & 0.03 \\ 0.03 & 0.09 \end{bmatrix}$ m² for $(x, y)$. Give σ_x, σ_y and ρ. In words, what does the sign of ρ tell you about the shape of the ellipse?

### Exercise FM.15-E2 — Ellipse by hand `[numerical]`

Goal: connect eigenvalues to the ellipse you see in RViz.
For $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\times10^{-4}$ m², find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors by hand (hint: try $[1, 1]$ and $[1, -1]$), then the σ along each axis and the 95% ellipse semi-axes in mm. Check with `np.linalg.eigh`.

### Exercise FM.15-E3 — Turn the robot `[predict]`

Goal: build intuition for $R\Sigma R^\top$.
In the robot frame after driving 1 m the covariance is $\operatorname{diag}(1.00\times10^{-4},\ 1.2185\times10^{-3})$ m². **Predict before computing**: what is the world-frame covariance when the robot's heading is 90°? Then compute it for 90° and 30°, and give ρ for 30°.

### Exercise FM.15-E4 — When linearization breaks `[coding]`

Goal: know when $J\Sigma J^\top$ is trustworthy.
Using `drive_straight_mc` and `drive_straight_linearized` with $d = 2.0$ m, $\sigma_d = 10$ mm, heading 0, `np.random.default_rng(seed=5)` and 200,000 samples, compare Monte Carlo and linearized mean and covariance for $\sigma_\theta = 2°$ and for $\sigma_\theta = 0.3$ rad (17°). For each, also report the fraction of samples inside the linearized 95% ellipse. Plot the second case: what shape is the cloud?

### Exercise FM.15-E5 — The config file that crashes the particle filter `[debugging]`

Goal: validate covariance matrices before using them.
A YAML config sets the initial pose covariance to `[[0.01, 0.02], [0.02, 0.01]]` m². `np.linalg.cholesky` raises an error when the particle filter initializes. What error, what is wrong with the matrix (give its eigenvalues and implied ρ), and write a `validate_covariance(S) -> None` function that raises a clear message for non-symmetric or non-PSD matrices.

## Expected result

- **FM.15-E1:** σ_x = 0.20 m, σ_y = 0.30 m, ρ = 0.03/0.06 = 0.50. Positive ρ: the ellipse tilts "up-right" — when x is too large, y tends to be too large.
- **FM.15-E2:** eigenvalues $8\times10^{-4}$ (eigenvector $[1,1]/\sqrt2$, 45°) and $2\times10^{-4}$ (eigenvector $[1,-1]/\sqrt2$, 135°, sign may be flipped by numpy). σ along axes: 28.3 mm and 14.1 mm. 95% semi-axes: 69.2 mm (along 45°) and 34.6 mm (along 135°).
- **FM.15-E3:** heading 90°: $\operatorname{diag}(1.2185\times10^{-3},\ 1.00\times10^{-4})$ — the variances swap, because "sideways" is now along world x. Heading 30°: $\begin{bmatrix} 3.796 & -4.843 \\ -4.843 & 9.389 \end{bmatrix}\times10^{-4}$ m², ρ = −0.811.
- **FM.15-E4:** σ_θ = 2°: MC mean ≈ (1.9988, 0.0000), MC cov ≈ diag(1.03e-4, 4.85e-3), linearized diag(1.00e-4, 4.87e-3), inside-ellipse fraction ≈ 0.946 — linearization is fine. σ_θ = 0.3 rad: MC mean x ≈ 1.912 m (88 mm short of the linearized 2.000), MC var x ≈ 0.0149 m² vs linearized 0.0001 (≈150× larger), var y ≈ 0.33 vs 0.36, and only ≈ 38% of samples are inside the "95%" ellipse. The cloud is a curved banana (an arc of radius 2 m), which no ellipse can represent. This is why EKFs struggle with large heading uncertainty and particle filters don't ([10.08](../../10-localization/10.08-particle-filter-mcl.md)).
- **FM.15-E5:** `numpy.linalg.LinAlgError: Matrix is not positive definite`. Eigenvalues are 0.03 and −0.01 (a negative variance along the 135° direction); implied ρ = 0.02/√(0.01·0.01) = 2.0 > 1. Your validator should check `np.allclose(S, S.T)` and `np.linalg.eigvalsh(S).min() >= -1e-12`, and the message should name the offending eigenvalue. A valid version, e.g. `[[0.01, 0.005], [0.005, 0.01]]` (ρ = 0.5), passes.

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: Monte Carlo covariance and $J\Sigma J^\top$ disagree

1. Check the sample count: sample covariance entries have relative error around $\sqrt{2/N}$ (≈ 0.5% for 100,000). Differences at that level are noise.
2. Check the Jacobian numerically: perturb each input by a small $h$ and compare $(f(x+h)-f(x-h))/2h$ to your analytic column ([FM.17](FM.17-derivatives.md)). Wrong signs on $-d\sin\theta$ are the classic bug.
3. Check units: σ_θ in degrees instead of radians inflates the sideways variance by $57.3^2 \approx 3283$×.
4. If the Jacobian is right and the gap grows with input σ, the function is too nonlinear over the uncertainty range (E4). Use Monte Carlo, an unscented transform, or a particle filter.

### Symptom: the drawn ellipse points the wrong way

1. `np.linalg.eig` does not sort eigenvalues; `eigh` sorts them ascending. Make sure you pair each eigenvalue with *its* eigenvector column (`eigvecs[:, i]`, a column, not a row).
2. Check the rotation direction: $R\Sigma R^\top$, not $R^\top\Sigma R$, when rotating robot-frame covariance into the world frame.
3. Check you're plotting with `ax.set_aspect("equal")`; otherwise ellipses look rotated.

### Symptom: Cholesky or `inv` fails on a covariance matrix

1. Print `np.linalg.eigvalsh(S)`. Slightly negative (−1e-18) means rounding: symmetrize `S = (S + S.T)/2` and add a tiny diagonal (1e-12).
2. Clearly negative means the matrix is invalid (E5): some |ρ| > 1, or entries typed in the wrong place (e.g. ROS 36-element array filled column-major or with the wrong index).
3. Exactly zero eigenvalue means a direction with no uncertainty (e.g. z for a ground robot). Use `pinv`, or put a small variance on that axis.

## Common mistakes

- **Summarizing a 2D estimate with σ_x and σ_y only.** You lose the correlation, and a diagonal ellipse can be badly wrong for a robot driving diagonally.
- **Using $k = 1$ for "the" uncertainty ellipse.** The 1-sigma ellipse contains only 39% of samples in 2D. Say which probability your ellipse shows.
- **Forgetting the transpose.** $J\Sigma$ is not a covariance; $J\Sigma J^\top$ is.
- **Degrees in covariance matrices.** ROS and all the math use radians and m²/rad².
- **All-zero covariance in a ROS message.** Consumers (robot_localization, Nav2) may treat it as infinite confidence or ignore it. Put realistic values.
- **Believing linearization everywhere.** Large heading uncertainty makes position clouds curved; check with Monte Carlo.

## Knowledge check

1. $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 0.25 & -0.1 \\ -0.1 & 0.16 \end{bmatrix}$. What are σ_x, σ_y and ρ?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   σ_x = 0.5, σ_y = 0.4, ρ = −0.1/(0.5·0.4) = −0.5. The ellipse tilts "up-left".
   </details>

2. Why must a covariance matrix be symmetric and positive semi-definite?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Symmetric because cov(X, Y) = cov(Y, X). PSD because $\mathbf{v}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{v}$ is the variance of the projection $\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{x}$, and a variance can't be negative.
   </details>

3. A robot drives 3 m with heading σ = 1° (0.01745 rad) and negligible distance error. Roughly what is the sideways σ at the end?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $d\cdot\sigma_\theta = 3 \cdot 0.01745 = 0.052$ m ≈ 5 cm. Heading error dominates long straight drives.
   </details>

4. Two observations are both 5 cm from the estimated position. One is accepted by the Mahalanobis gate, the other rejected. How is that possible?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The Mahalanobis distance divides by the uncertainty *in that direction*. Along the direction where σ is 35 mm, 5 cm is 1.4σ (accept); along the direction where σ is 10 mm, 5 cm is 5σ (reject).
   </details>

5. In a `geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovariance`, which array indices hold var x, cov(x, yaw) and var yaw?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Row-major 6×6 in order (x, y, z, rot X, rot Y, rot Z): var x = `[0]`, cov(x, yaw) = `[5]` (row 0, col 5) and `[30]` (row 5, col 0), var yaw = `[35]`.
   </details>

6. Predict: you rotate a covariance $\operatorname{diag}(a, a)$ (a circle) by 30°. What do you get?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $\operatorname{diag}(a, a)$ again: $R(aI)R^\top = a\,RR^\top = aI$. A circle has no preferred direction.
   </details>

7. Debugging: your EKF's position ellipse is tiny while the robot is clearly lost after a sharp turn with wheel slip. The Monte Carlo cloud of the same motion is banana-shaped. What is the underlying issue?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The EKF linearizes the motion around the mean; with large heading uncertainty the true distribution is curved and wider than $J\Sigma J^\top$ predicts (E4 showed 150× underestimated variance along x). The filter becomes overconfident. Remedies: larger process noise for turns, an unscented filter, or a particle filter.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Propagate a pose covariance through a whole trajectory. The robot state is $(x, y, \theta)$, the motion per step is "drive $\Delta d$, then turn $\Delta\theta$", with $\sigma_{\Delta d} = 0.02\,\Delta d$ and $\sigma_{\Delta\theta} = 0.05\,|\Delta\theta| + 0.002$ rad per step. Drive a 1 m × 1 m square (4 sides of 10 steps of 0.1 m each, a 90° turn after each side).

Acceptance criteria:
- You derive the 3×3 Jacobians of the pose update with respect to the state and to $(\Delta d, \Delta\theta)$, and propagate $\Sigma_{k+1} = F\Sigma_k F^\top + G\,Q\,G^\top$ over the 40 steps.
- A Monte Carlo run of 5,000 noisy squares agrees with your final 3×3 covariance within 10% on every diagonal entry.
- You plot the 95% ellipse at each corner of the square over the Monte Carlo dots, and explain why the ellipse at the end is larger than at the start even though the robot returned to its starting point.

(This is the prediction half of the EKF; you will finish it in [10.06](../../10-localization/10.06-extended-kalman-filter.md).)

## Go deeper

- https://cs229.stanford.edu/section/gaussians.pdf — Stanford CS229 section notes "The Multivariate Gaussian Distribution": short, rigorous, with the ellipse geometry.
- https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.cov.html — `np.cov` reference; note `rowvar` (the default treats each *row* as a variable, which surprises everyone once).
- https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/p/geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovariance.html — the ROS 2 Jazzy message definition with the covariance ordering.
- https://github.com/rlabbe/Kalman-and-Bayesian-Filters-in-Python — Labbe's chapter "Multivariate Gaussians" plots covariance ellipses and leads straight into the multivariate Kalman filter.
- https://kalmanfilter.net/ — numerical, step-by-step treatment of covariance propagation in Kalman filters.
- https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262201629/probabilistic-robotics/ — *Probabilistic Robotics*, chapters 3 and 5: Gaussian filters and the velocity/odometry motion models with their Jacobians.
